sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Following the November 3 midterm elections, data centre expansion emerged as a significant political issue. Voters in several states expressed strong opposition to new facilities, citing concerns over environmental damage, local community influence, and the potential for increased utility costs. Despite significant spending by pro-AI groups, candidates opposing rapid data centre development won seats in multiple states.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Data centres have become a focal point for public anxiety regarding AI and corporate power. Many residents feel excluded from planning processes, often due to outdated zoning laws or nondisclosure agreements. There is growing pressure for companies to fund their own infrastructure upgrades rather than passing costs to local communities.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Democratic control of Congress could facilitate new federal oversight, including potential moratoriums or stricter environmental guardrails. Analysts expect continued legislative efforts at both federal and local levels to regulate energy usage and land rights.

sections.text: President Santiago Peña stepped down after the insolvency of Ueno Bank caused widespread financial disruption. The bank, which held significant public funds and pensions, froze operations, preventing millions from accessing their money. Following accusations of misconduct and conflict of interest regarding his previous shareholding, the lower house of congress initiated impeachment proceedings. Peña stated he resigned to maintain social peace and democratic stability.

The situation threatened the stability of the government and required immediate intervention by the central bank to manage the crisis and address the needs of affected depositors.

Some sites also featured inaccurate details about repayment thresholds and write-off dates, while the Department for Education's website lacked real-world examples for Plan 5 students.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier said the information was misleading and compared repayments to minor expenses. Graduates may face higher monthly repayments as their salaries increase over time, meaning initial low estimates can give a false impression of future costs.

gist: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production in Texas around the middle of next year.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Tesla chief executive Elon Musk has announced that production of the Cybertruck will wind down around the middle of next year at its Texas factory. The vehicle launched in 2023 but suffered from disappointing sales, quality issues, delays, and recalls, failing to approach its target of 200,000 annual sales.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The decision marks the end of Tesla's attempt to capture the US pickup market. The Cybertruck never went on sale in Europe after failing to meet safety standards. Musk is now prioritising artificial intelligence, robotics, and autonomous driving over traditional vehicle development.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tesla will use its factory in Austin, Texas to expand Cybercab production and build the Optimus humanoid robot. The company is also ramping up production of its Semi electric lorry and aims to begin Roadster production in 2028.

quotes.text: We dug our own grave with Cybertruck

gist: Tube drivers in the RMT union announced 24-hour strikes over working arrangements.
The industrial action is in opposition to Transport for London plans for a four-day week.
Business groups warned the Christmas run-up strikes would cause significant disruption to commuters and shoppers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: London Underground drivers in the RMT union announced a series of 24-hour strikes starting on 26 November, with further walkouts planned through December, January and February. The action is in dispute over plans for a voluntary four-day working week, which the RMT opposes. Meanwhile, the Aslef union welcomed the proposals, calling the strike a strange choice.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The RMT argued the plans would worsen shift times, increase driving hours and pave the way for job cuts. Transport for London maintained the changes are voluntary, offer a choice of working pattern, and reduce overall hours. Business groups warned the strikes risk damaging the hospitality sector and vital Christmas trading.

fivew: Tube drivers in the RMT union.

In opposition to plans to introduce a four-day working week.

quotes.text: London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers' working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.
This will give our colleagues a real, meaningful choice on their working pattern without having to change where they work.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Amazon launched a feature allowing selected US customers to text the Alexa shopping assistant. Users can send text messages or photographs of items to search for products, manage lists, compare prices, and complete purchases.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The feature taps into a growing trend of interacting with AI agents through text messages ahead of the holiday shopping season. It follows Amazon blocking another tool in September and competes with similar text-based shopping features from other companies.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Following the initial rollout to a small group, Amazon plans to expand the texting capability to millions more customers in the upcoming weeks. Those without an invite can join a waitlist.

gist: A childminder who left over 20 children unattended was jailed for two years.
Suspicious parents discovered the neglect after watching her leave for a school run.
An internal probe revealed she was likely tipped off about previous inspections.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Amanda Mathewson, a childminder in Dunfermline, was jailed for two years after pleading guilty to wilfully neglecting and abandoning children. Suspicious parents watched her leave for a school run and found over 20 unattended children inside her home in August 2024. Children were found unsupervised, distressed, and in hot rooms without food or water.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case exposed a gross abuse of trust and severe regulatory failings. The Care Inspectorate admitted Mathewson was likely tipped off about inspections by an insider, compromising regulatory scrutiny and leading families to explore civil action.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A learning review by the Fife child protection committee will examine potential improvements to practice and processes. The Scottish government is working with independent regulators to enhance transparency, while lawyers represent families exploring a civil case.

fivew: A childminder was jailed for two years for leaving more than 20 children alone and unsupervised.
She pleaded guilty to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children to unnecessary suffering.

gist: David Staff has died aged 68 of a heart condition.

His former apprentice will continue the Suffolk workshop.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: David Staff, a cornetto player, period trumpeter and maker of natural trumpets, has died aged 68 of a heart condition. He learned instrument making from Frank Tomes, eventually taking over the business and establishing a workshop near Coddenham in Suffolk. Staff was also a founder member of His Majestys Sagbutts & Cornetts and a long-serving principal trumpet in the Orchestra of the Eighteenth Century.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Staff was a significant figure in the early music revival of the late 20th century. He was widely respected for his high-register playing, refined interpretations, and his craft in making natural trumpets from flat sheets of brass. He also made a major contribution to music education, teaching at the Royal Northern College of Music and the Conservatorium van Amsterdam.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The workshop will be continued by his former apprentice and hand engraver of 11 years.

gist: Prince Harry and five others are appealing against a High Court privacy ruling.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prince Harry, Sir Elton John, David Furnish, Elizabeth Hurley, Sadie Frost and Baroness Lawrence have applied to appeal a High Court ruling dismissing their privacy case against Associated Newspapers. Following an 11-week trial, Mr Justice Nicklin ruled the claimants had failed to prove that journalists used unlawful information gathering. The judge ordered them to pay an initial £9.54m in legal costs.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Associated Newspapers described the judgement as an overwhelming victory for its journalists, who denied illegal activity and cited legitimate sourcing. Harry and Lawrence described the verdict as a whitewash, whilst the claimants consider the rulings legally and factually flawed. Outlets differed on total costs: the BBC cited costs up to £34.5m, whereas The Guardian reported over £50m.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Applications have been filed with the Court of Appeal for permission to challenge the dismissal of claims and the indemnity costs order.

articles.standfirst: The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds

timeline.text: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

gist: Scientists discovered that enjoyable conversations exhibit a healthy dose of pink noise.
Pink noise represents a conversational balance between stability and conversational flexibility.
The research analysed conversations between strangers, friends, speed-daters, and podcasts.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Researchers at Dartmouth College analysed over 1,000 conversations between strangers answering questions, as well as chats between friends and speed-dating pairs. They used an artificial intelligence program named MPNet to score turns in the conversations across 768 criteria.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Conversations exhibiting pink noise were found to be more enjoyable, fostered stronger connections, and predicted whether speed-daters would meet again. This provides fresh insights into what creates a satisfying exchange, moving beyond simple similarity.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: While defining a great chat remains tricky, researchers suspect that the conversational skill required to produce pink noise can be learned and developed over time.

fivew: Scientists discovered that a healthy dose of pink noise is the secret to a satisfying conversation.
To find fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.

quotes.text: In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.
In sync can be incredibly dull

The policy stops police from contacting ICE over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses.
The decision follows recent midterm elections and local incidents involving ICE agents.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Houston's mayor, John Whitmire, announced that the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Under the new directive, police will not contact ICE over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses or traffic incidents. Police should only contact ICE if an individual is arrested on a jailable charge or if ICE issues an administrative warrant.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The move is one of the first steps to curb ICE's powers following midterm elections and aims to reduce fear and anxiety among residents. ICE remains dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The immigrant-rights group Fiel Houston planned to hold a press conference following the mayor's announcement to follow through on local decisions.

timeline.text: Man unexpectedly recovers from a knife wound through his eye and brain

gist: A man made an unexpected and rapid recovery after a knife penetrated his eye and brain.
Doctors noted that the exact mechanism of his injury remains unclear, noting a history of depression.
Such low-velocity penetrating brain injuries carry high risks, yet fortunate recoveries have been documented historically.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A man suffered a knife wound through his eye and brain. Following intensive care and surgery to remove his breathing tube, he recovered rapidly. Scans showed healing with minor bleeding, swelling, and air in the brain tissue, but no infections or seizures occurred. His language function was preserved, and temporary right-side weakness resolved quickly. He was later discharged and remained well at follow-up appointments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Injuries going through the eye and brain are rare and typically involve high-velocity mechanisms like gunshots. Knives are rarer low-velocity mechanisms that carry substantial morbidity and mortality. This case highlights that outcomes may depend on precise trajectory relative to critical structures rather than external severity.

gist: Over three months after a massive Cairngorms fire, the writer visits the charred landscape.
Volunteers plant thousands of native montane trees in an affected glen to aid restoration.
New green shoots, ferns, and fire-loving fungi are beginning to emerge amidst the devastation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A severe moorland and forest fire engulfed 25 square kilometres in the Cairngorms. Months later, the writer visited the charred area, noting widespread blackness, charcoal pines, and ongoing dangers like falling trees and hotspots. Despite the damage, some areas show surprising resilience with blooming bog asphodel and active black grouse.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The fire drastically altered the landscape, destroying thick heather and damaging roots and peat in the forest. However, restoration efforts are underway as a group planted over 3,000 native montane trees grown from nearby seeds. Additionally, natural regeneration is visible through emerging deer-grass, birch shoots, bracken, and fire-loving fungi.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Landscape restoration programmes will continue in the area, supported by ongoing tree-planting initiatives and the natural emergence of new growth and pyrophilous fungi in the charcoal.

gist: Luke Alfano founded Too Young to Grieve to support young adults experiencing loss.
The grief support community operates in over 20 locations, including a new Belfast branch.
Members share experiences through activities such as walks, hikes, football, and pottery painting.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Luke Alfano set up Too Young to Grieve, a support community offering young people aged 18 to 35 a space to talk about loss. Founded after Alfano lost his father and grandmother, the group has expanded to more than 20 locations, including London, Manchester, the US, Australia, and Belfast. Members meet for activities such as walks, pottery painting, and football tournaments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Young adults often feel isolated when facing bereavement because few peers share their experience. Members like Chris Guiller, Katherine Macauley, and William Gregg say the community helps them realise they are not alone and gives them a safe space to process grief and protect their mental health.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Statutory guidance published by the Department for Education requires primary and secondary school lessons on loss and bereavement from September 2026. However, Northern Ireland does not have equivalent statutory guidance, relying instead on pastoral care policies and curriculum resources.

timeline.text: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

gist: A report shows Anthropic is using AI to accelerate its own development rapidly.
The company heavily redacted the published findings, prompting criticism over transparency.
Researchers express alarm that recursive self-improvement may happen faster than expected.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An investigative report by METR revealed that Anthropic is using artificial intelligence to build better systems at twice the speed seen last year. Employees reported massive productivity boosts when using these internal tools. Although Anthropic gave researchers broad access, the company heavily redacted the final public document to protect commercial secrets and prevent rivals from copying its methods.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The findings challenge previous timelines regarding how soon artificial intelligence might improve itself without human help. Critics highlighted a contradiction between the company calling for caution in the industry while simultaneously speeding up its own research. Furthermore, the extensive redactions sparked concern that the public lacks sufficient information to assess the risks properly.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Anthropic plans to release its own evaluation regarding development speeds soon alongside new safety measures. Meanwhile, lawmakers and researchers are increasing pressure for stricter oversight, and some officials are urging legislative bodies to consider banning recursive self-improvement entirely.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Catastrophic floods hit Nepal on 26 August, wiping away whole villages and leaving 1,459 dead and 5,285 unaccounted for, including more than 700 foreigners. Nepal officially ended the active search-and-rescue operation last month, moving into a search-and-rehabilitation phase.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Families of missing locals and foreigners have spent 10 weeks without answers, facing unbearable uncertainty. Rebuilding will cost nearly US$4.78bn, and tourism has dropped off, impacting the country's GDP.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Authorities will recover any remains, property, or valuables found during the rehabilitation process. Governments are working to issue death certificates, and DNA testing is matching families with remains.

Archaeologists recovered numerous artefacts including brooches, coins, and pottery before homes were built.
The findings change previous historical beliefs about relations between Romans and local populations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Archaeologists uncovered a 2,000-year-old Roman settlement containing a jewellery workshop beneath a housing development in Mancot, Flintshire. Researchers removed items such as pottery, coins, and brooches before houses were built on the Gladstone Way site.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The discovery challenges past theories suggesting poor relations between Romans and native populations in north-east Wales. Items found suggest local industry, trade reaching mainland Europe, and long-term occupation stretching back to the Iron Age.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Artefacts will undergo conservation and analysis at the National Museum of Wales in Cardiff. Officials plan to display items locally, with hopes they could reach Mold Museum by 2027.

gist: New Zealand voted in a new government amid a pervasive mood of national apathy and dread.
Economic struggles, high living costs and job shortages are driving a record-breaking exodus of citizens.
Disillusionment and declining trust in political and social institutions are creating a crisis of confidence.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: New Zealand held an election for a new government on Saturday, with voters showing widespread apathy, exhaustion and disillusionment. Voters deserted the two major parties in record numbers, while smaller parties across the political spectrum gained support.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A low national mood and falling trust in leaders reflect deep economic and social pressures. High inflation, expensive housing, a tough job market for young people and healthcare crises are damaging living standards and driving a record number of people to leave the country daily.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The newly elected government must address widespread material hardship, social polarisation and a shrinking talent pool as citizens continue to question the country's future direction.

timeline.text: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers

gist: Democrats won midterm elections, causing potential roadblocks for data centers and tech companies.
Voters rejected data center measures and elected politicians who promised to restrict them.
OpenAI changed policies, dropping NDAs and releasing a compute campus policy blueprint.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Democrats won the midterms in a historic victory. Voters rejected ballot measures regarding data centers and elected politicians like Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa who promised restrictions. Elon Musk donated heavily to Republicans, but now finds his companies in a blue state.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Data centers have become a grassroots issue due to secrecy, NDAs, and environmental concerns like water scarcity. Tech companies and hyperscalers now face tougher regulatory roadblocks and changing financial incentives from Wall Street.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tech companies face more difficult conditions over the next two years and beyond. OpenAI has responded by changing policies, dropping requirements for NDAs, and introducing a compute campus policy blueprint to rebrand data centers.

fivew: Tech companies, hyperscalers, Elon Musk, and politicians like Gina Hinojosa.
Due to grassroots backlash against secretive data center approvals, environmental concerns, and water scarcity.

sections.heading: What happens next

gist: Flesh won the final series of Drag Race UK broadcast by the BBC.
The BBC cancelled the programme as a result of financial pressures and budget cuts.
The show will move to a streaming platform run by its production company.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: RuPaul crowned London performer Flesh as the series eight winner following the final episode. Twelve contestants competed throughout ten weeks before the broadcaster announced the cancellation of the series due to budget cuts. Flesh received a cash prize of £25,000.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The programme will transition to a subscription streaming service owned by the production company, which causes worries about reduced audiences and fewer opportunities for performers. Some fans hope the move might bring larger cash prizes.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The UK edition of the series will move to Wow Presents Plus, marking a new chapter for the programme after its departure from the BBC.

fivew: RuPaul crowned a new winner as the BBC cancelled the UK series.
The BBC decided to axe the programme because of financial pressures and budget cuts.

quotes.text: This is where it feels slightly sadder that we're leaving the BBC because for all of the parameters that it created that limited what we could do, there was more exposure than drag has ever been given

timeline.text: England 'disappointment' fuels Dewsbury-Hall's Everton heroics

gist: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall responded to missing out on the England squad with a brilliant performance.
His thunderous strike helped Everton to a comeback victory over Coventry City.
Thierno Barry also scored twice to help secure a three-one win for Everton.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Everton secured a three-one comeback victory over Coventry City at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall scored a thunderous strike after learning he was overlooked for the England squad by Thomas Tuchel. Thierno Barry scored twice in five minutes at the start of the second half.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The win lifted Everton to fifth in the Premier League table and marked back-to-back league wins. For Dewsbury-Hall, the performance was a strong response to his England disappointment. Barry took his season tally to ten goals in all competitions, continuing his impressive goalscoring form under David Moyes.

fivew: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Thierno Barry starred for Everton.
Everton secured a three-one comeback victory over Coventry City.
Dewsbury-Hall was fueled by his disappointment at missing out on the England squad.

quotes.text: It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie.
I'm really, really enjoying it.

Altrincham have defeated 17 Football League teams, more than any other non-league club.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Non-league side Altrincham are preparing to face League One club Notts County in the FA Cup. Former player and manager Graham Heathcote highlighted the club's proud history of defeating 17 Football League opponents, while current manager Neil Gibson hopes to write a new chapter.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Altrincham hold the record for defeating the most Football League sides as a dedicated non-league team. Achieving another upset would reinforce their identity as cup giant-killers and boost their standing in an area dominated by larger Manchester clubs.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Altrincham will play Notts County at Moss Lane on Saturday in front of a live BBC television audience.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Manchester City fell to a 3-1 defeat against Forest at the City Ground after conceding early and failing to match their opponents' intensity. Individual defensive errors cost City dearly, leading to three consecutive Premier League losses.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The defeat leaves City six points behind the champions heading into the international break. History shows that overcoming a six-point deficit after ten games is rare, while defensive frailties and ongoing financial rule appeals add pressure to Enzo Maresca's campaign.

New Zealand dominated the second half with superior rugby IQ and physicality.
Scotland's defensive frailties were once again exposed by elite opponents.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: New Zealand defeated Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield after a close first half that saw Ewan Ashman score a hat-trick for Scotland. The All Blacks took control in the second half, securing a systematic dismantling finished off by Beauden Barrett's second try.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The match highlighted Scotland's recurring defensive frailties against elite teams. While Scotland's attack can challenge the best, their inability to stop tries prevents them from closing the gap against top-tier rugby nations like New Zealand.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Gregor Townsend must repair his team's shattered morale ahead of next Sunday's match against the Wallabies, while Australia will look to exploit Scotland's exposed defensive weaknesses.

fivew: New Zealand defeated Scotland in a rugby union match.
New Zealand increased their intensity and accuracy in the second half to exploit Scotland's defensive frailties.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Sao Paulo Grand Prix marks the start of the final phase of the championship. Mercedes aims to secure the constructors' title. Meanwhile, Ferrari held clear-the-air talks following tension between team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after they tangled on the first lap in Mexico.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Positions in the standings affect prize money and provide motivation for next season. sections.heading: What happens next

timeline.text: Norris takes pole in rain-delayed qualifying

gist: Lando Norris took pole for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix in wet conditions.
Qualifying at Interlagos was delayed for nearly an hour and a half due to heavy rain.
Engine-related grid penalties significantly reshaped the starting grid for the race.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Lando Norris secured pole position for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix during a rain-delayed qualifying session at Interlagos. Heavy rain delayed the start by an hour and a half. Wet conditions allowed drivers in usually uncompetitive cars to perform well, while several drivers incurred grid penalties for engine parts.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The wet weather levelled the playing field, allowing drivers like Fernando Alonso, Oliver Bearman, Nico Hulkenberg and Liam Lawson to achieve some of their best qualifying results of the year. Grid penalties for drivers including George Russell, Charles Leclerc, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton also changed the final starting lineup.

sections.text: Martin Odegaard scored a 72nd-minute goal to secure a 1-0 win for Arsenal against Hull. A penalty was initially expected for a shirt pull on Kai Havertz, but the referee pivoted to an offside decision after a VAR review.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The incident highlighted ongoing confusion and debate surrounding VAR interpretations of fouls versus offside offences. Arsenal secured three points to remain Premier League leaders, though their attack continues to lack fluency.
